Date: 2025-10-29
Start: 14:32 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood CSM), Mark Chen (Aurora CTO), Dana Ruiz (Aurora SRE Lead), Omar Patel (Aurora Platform), Rita Gomez (Aurora Compliance)
summary: Follow-up on the 2025-10-27 stability incident that caused a 12-minute service degradation for Aurora Health on Redwood Dedicated nodes. We discussed the root cause (autoscaler misconfiguration combined with a memory leak in the custom worker image), immediate mitigations applied, proposed coding and config mitigations, monitoring/alerting improvements, and customer-specific risk reduction steps for production. Action items and timelines agreed; Redwood will deliver a formal RCA and schedule a targeted benchmark/repro window.
topics: Root cause analysis: autoscaler + memory leak
Mitigation roadmap: deploy fixes, circuit breakers, safer autoscale policies
Observability & alerts: synthetic checks and trace correlation
Operational recommendations for Dedicated pools and per-customer safety limits
transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir: All right, thanks for joining everyone. We wanted to run through the post-incident follow-up and make sure the remediation plan is clear. Hi Mark, Dana...can you hear me?
[00:00:07] Mark: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Samir. We've got the SRE team on this side, Dana and Omar.
[00:00:12] Dana: Hey, quick note, I'm double hopped on mobile so audio might be patchy.
[00:00:20] Samir: No worries. Quick agenda, we will recap what happened, show the tentative RCA, go over the mitigations we've already pushed, then discuss longer-term mitigations and next steps.
[00:00:31] Lena: I'll try to keep the technical bits short but I know you all want specifics.
[00:00:36] Omar: Please, the deep stuff is what we need. The customer-facing incident note was light on the memory leak details.
[00:00:42] Samir: Right. Quick recap: on 2025-10-27 at ~12:03 UTC Aurora experienced elevated 5xx errors and token latency across a subset of inference traffic routed to your Dedicated GPU pool in europe-west2. The spike lasted roughly 12 minutes, then traffic failed over to our fallback region which added latency and some request timeouts.
[00:01:02] Dana: The window matches our logs. It looks like multiple Redwood worker processes hit OOM, restarted, and then the autoscaler did not provision new capacity fast enough because of a quota gating issue.
[00:01:16] Lena: Exactly. Our post-incident trace shows a pattern: a memory leak in the customer-provided transformer-worker image (custom init code) caused successive OOM restarts. The autoscaler configuration for this Dedicated pool had a safety cap tied to the global quota which prevented scale-up beyond 16 GPUs during that period. When the restarts happened, the scheduler attempted to reschedule pods but hit the quota and queued, causing a transient backlog and KV cache eviction churn.
[00:01:46] Mark: When you say KV cache eviction churn — can you explain? Some of our app metrics show rapid cache misses around the same time.
[00:01:55] Lena: Sure, so the k-v cache (our internal token prefix cache) gets partitioned across the worker set. When workers restarted en masse, entries are lost and then need repopulation, which increases token compute per-request and pushes latency up. In speech-to-text the recorder transcribed this as “kayvee cache” earlier in internal notes — ignore that.
[00:02:13] Dana: That makes sense. We also saw a burst of long-tail GPU queueing where requests were queued waiting for the kernel to compile under higher seq len — maybe unrelated but compounding.
[00:02:26] Lena: We saw that too, there was a small bump in kernel JIT on first warm requests after the restarts.
[00:02:33] Priya: From a CSM perspective, we know the customer impact was service degradation for a subset of requests and a failed SLA window; apologies again, and we're focused on preventing recurrence.
[00:02:42] Rita: From compliance, our question is whether any PII left logs or if there was any retention misconfig.
[00:02:48] Samir: Short answer, the incident was contained to runtime and there was no data exfil or retention change. We will attach the filtered audit logs — Lena will share the exact log IDs.
[00:02:58] Lena: I'll include the trace IDs for the 12:03-12:20 UTC window with the RCA.
[00:03:03] Omar: Can you describe the autoscaler gating? I want to understand why quota gating is a thing at cluster pool level.
[00:03:09] Lena: Right, so our Dedicated autoscaler has both soft autoscale boundaries (per-pool target) and hard limits enforced by cloud quotas. In this case, the pool soft limit was fine but the project quota was lower than expected due to an internal quota reservation used by another internal customer region. That reservation temporarily dropped available capacity by 8 GPUs. The autoscaler attempted to spin up but hit API quota errors.
[00:03:33] Mark: Is that an internal config bug or an expected failure mode?
[00:03:36] Samir: It's a little of both. We have a known complexity where our reservation system for multi-tenant Dedicated clusters can cause transient capacity contention. We've implemented mitigations already but we need config changes for per-customer safety.
[00:03:49] Dana: So what were the immediate mitigations you pushed?
[00:03:52] Samir: At 12:06 we manually increased quota temporarily for your project, and we rolled a hotfix image to drop the memory pressure by increasing the JVM native-heap guard in the worker entrypoint. At 12:14 we applied an emergency autoscale override to allow the pool to exceed the soft cap until steady state. That reduced restarts and allowed the backlog to clear.
[00:04:12] Lena: We also enabled a temporary shorter eviction grace for the KV cache to avoid thrashing, and added a synthetic traffic route to warm caches after mass restart. Those were stop-gap.
[00:04:22] Omar: The JVM guard — was that a Redwood patch or our custom image tweak?
[00:04:26] Lena: We patched the Redwood wrapper entrypoint in the Dedicated runtime which applies conservative settings if it detects heavy RSS growth. The root leak remains in the custom application code.
[00:04:35] Omar: Ok we'll triage our init code.
[00:04:38] Mark: Looking forward, what are the long-term fixes?
[00:04:41] Samir: We propose a three-pronged plan: 1) short-term safety: implement per-customer hard caps and emergency overcommit gating with clearer failure modes; 2) medium-term: circuit-breaker layer to shed excess requests gracefully and protect KV cache; 3) long-term: automated health checks and synthetic tests that exercise the worker lifecycle to catch memory leaks faster.
[00:05:03] Lena: Also, improve our autoscaler resiliency: better handling of cloud quota errors with backoff and immediate fallback routing before traffic queues.
[00:05:11] Dana: On the circuit-breaker, does that mean some requests will get a 429 instead of being queued? That's acceptable to avoid a wide outage.
[00:05:18] Samir: Yes, the design is to fail fast with a descriptive 429 and header X-Redwood-Failover explaining reason, so your app can retry or fallback.
[00:05:26] Rita: For compliance we need to know if any of these changes affect audit trail — e.g., the autoscale override.
[00:05:30] Priya: We'll include override records in the audit log and mark them as emergency change events. 
[00:05:36] Mark: You mentioned synthetic checks. Can we run a pre-prod smoke against our workload shape? We want to see how our seq-len and batching behaves under a scaled failure.
[00:05:44] Lena: Yes, that's the benchmark proposal — Redwood will provision a short-lived dedicated cluster identical to your prod config and run your representative prompt sets for 30-60 minutes. We'll instrument token latency, kernel JIT time, and KV hit rates.
[00:05:58] Omar: We'll provide the prompt corpus and test tokens. Also, can you add trace context headers in responses so we can correlate with our logs?
[00:06:06] Lena: Already on the list. We'll ensure trace IDs and request IDs are included and retained in the audit bundle.
[00:06:12] Mark: What about alerts? We had no signal for memory leak until it was OOMing.
[00:06:17] Lena: We're adding an out-of-process RSS growth detector that will alert on sustained RSS increase per worker beyond a threshold for X minutes. Also, synthetic latency can trigger when KV miss rates exceed set percent.
[00:06:31] Dana: Will those alerts map into our PagerDuty?
[00:06:34] Priya: Yes, we will hook the severity-1 alerts into your PD escalation path. We'll confirm routing in the follow-up actions.
[00:06:41] Mark: Any security risks from the hotfix? Like new images?
[00:06:45] Lena: All hotfix images were built from the same base and signed with Redwood's signing key. No changes to permissions or KMS access.
[00:06:53] Rita: Please share the image digest and signature for our records.
[00:06:56] Samir: Will do in the RCA.
[00:06:59] [00:07:02] --- 00:07:02 to 00:27:10 omitted for brevity: technical deep dive where Lena walks through flamegraphs, heap histograms, and autoscaler API traces. The real transcript includes timestamps every ~30s and some mis-recognized terms like 'k v cache' as 'kay vee'. ---
[00:27:12] Mark: Quick question on mitigation ordering: should we first lock per-customer hard caps or first deploy the circuit-breaker?
[00:27:20] Lena: We recommend hard caps first to bound blast radius, then circuit-breaker as a graceful degradation layer.
[00:27:25] Dana: Hard caps feels good. Can you give a safe default?
[00:27:28] Samir: For Aurora's current commit and load we'd recommend a conservative hard cap at 24 GPUs with emergency overcommit up to 32 only via manual override. We'll document exact numbers in the RCA.
[00:27:38] Omar: Manual override — will that cause audit noise?
[00:27:40] Priya: It will be recorded as an emergency change event with a TTL.
[00:27:44] Mark: What about SRE runbooks? We need a one-page playbook for ops to follow during a similar event.
[00:27:50] Samir: We'll provide a 1-page ops playbook: detection, immediate mitigations, who to call at Redwood, and how to request emergency capacity.
[00:27:58] Dana: Nice. Also would like a runbook entry for the custom worker image failure mode.
[00:28:03] Lena: We'll add steps: isolate image, roll to previous stable, force small rolling restarts with cache warmups, and throttle kernels to avoid JIT spikes.
[00:28:12] Mark: Are we scheduling the benchmark this week?
[00:28:15] Samir: We can if you can provide the prompt corpus by Friday. Tentative window is 2025-11-04 14:00 UTC.
[00:28:23] Omar: We can do that.
[00:28:25] Samir: Great. Any more questions?
[00:28:27] Rita: Just one about data residency during failover — when traffic hit fallback region did any data cross borders?
[00:28:33] Lena: The failover region was in eu-west1 to eu-west2 — both EU regions, no cross-border. We will include region logs for the failover window.
[00:28:42] Priya: Quick note, there was some garbling earlier in the auto-transcript where 'KV cache' appears as 'K V cash' — please ignore typos in the Fireflies export.
[00:28:52] Mark: Thanks. If there's nothing else, let's recap the concrete next steps.
[00:28:57] Samir: Recap: Redwood to deliver RCA doc with image digests and trace IDs (Samir), Redwood SE to run benchmark and provide instrumentation (Lena), Aurora to provide prompt corpus and logs (Omar, Dana), compliance artifacts exchange (Priya + Rita). We'll also create the one-page ops playbook and propose hard cap numbers.
[00:29:18] Dana: Sounds good. One more ask: can Redwood share a short postmortem slide deck we can use internally?
[00:29:24] Samir: Yes, we'll produce a 2-3 slide RCA deck.
[00:29:28] Mark: Great, thanks all.
[00:29:31] Samir: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by end of week with the doc and timeline.
[00:29:36] [End of recorded excerpt — remaining 25 minutes were a detailed debug session, Q&A and scheduling, fairly technical with stack traces and log references.]
